title: Does Your Professional Liability Insurance Cover AI Mistakes? Don't Be So Sure
author: Danielle Braff

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core account that generative AI can accelerate bounded legal work while introducing reliability risks. It materially extends the synthesis by identifying professional-liability and cyber-insurance coverage as an additional organisational risk-management issue, with protection uncertain and dependent on policy wording.
qs: Sure, AI can speed up mundane tasks and reduce lawyer workload.

Despite dispelling the cautionary tales of law firm AI usage, there is still no grand plan for insurance that would cover law firms and attorneys against any discrepancies that generative AI may be adding to their work.

st.t: Malpractice insurance: Reported AI claims remain hard to isolate
st.an: Braff accepts the cluster’s central uncertainty and materially develops it through policy-specific analysis: conventional malpractice and cyber coverage may leave gaps, while dedicated AI products are tailored through system-level due diligence and individualized terms. The article adds useful coverage and underwriting detail but does not establish AI-malpractice incidence or isolate AI’s contribution to losses.
qs: But “as with all policies, the devil is in the details of the specific terms and conditions of a policy to determine scope of coverage.”
Their AI insurance is available across the board—including for law firms—but the individual process to gain coverage includes due diligence on the AI systems used.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Braff accepts the cluster’s premise that legal AI offers task-level efficiency while creating reliability risks, then materially extends its governance analysis to professional and cyber liability coverage. She argues firms should not assume AI-related mistakes are insured and must assess the specific terms and conditions of their policies.
qs: But it also can be unreliable, and it is frequently disparaged for its hallucinations, biases and incomplete responses.
But “as with all policies, the devil is in the details of the specific terms and conditions of a policy to determine scope of coverage.”

st.t: AI insurance: Coverage cannot replace professional governance
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster’s principal proposition by treating AI insurance as conditional on specific policy wording, exclusions, sublimits and underwriting due diligence rather than as comprehensive protection. It also confirms that limited loss data constrain underwriting and recommends security controls, vendor scrutiny and coordination across policy lines, reinforcing that coverage complements rather than replaces governance.
qs: But “as with all policies, the devil is in the details of the specific terms and conditions of a policy to determine scope of coverage.”
They don’t have that amount of data on the frequency and severity of AI-related losses, Kalinich says.

kp.k: Law firms are rapidly funding generative AI
kp.d: The article reports substantial generative-AI investment among large US law firms: a February 2024 LexisNexis survey found that 43% of Am Law 200 firms had dedicated budgets for generative AI tools. It frames this adoption as potentially reducing mundane work and lawyer workload while introducing reliability risks.
qs: Lawyers have adopted generative artificial intelligence at a rapid pace.
According to a February 2024 LexisNexis survey, 43% of the Am Law 200 firms had a dedicated budget for investing in generative AI tools.
Sure, AI can speed up mundane tasks and reduce lawyer workload. But it also can be unreliable, and it is frequently disparaged for its hallucinations, biases and incomplete responses.

kp.k: Existing policies may not cover AI-related legal claims
kp.d: Lynda Bennett warns that professional liability coverage depends on each policy’s specific wording. AI-related claims may fall outside the definition of professional services or covered losses, particularly where a lawyer is sanctioned for using an AI tool; cyber policies may provide some protection, but their terms vary considerably.
qs: But “as with all policies, the devil is in the details of the specific terms and conditions of a policy to determine scope of coverage.”
Some lawyers may be surprised, after a claim is presented, to learn that coverage for AI-related claims is not explicitly covered by their malpractice policy.
Use of AI tools may not satisfy the definition of professional service or losses flowing from the use of such tools—particularly if lawyers are sanctioned based on the use of the tool, Bennett says.
“Lawyers may find the coverage that they need in their cyber policies, [but] we are still seeing tremendous variation among the terms and conditions of the coverage offered,” Bennett says.

kp.k: Insurers constrain AI exposure through exclusions and sublimits
kp.d: The article explains that insurers may manage AI risk either by excluding it or sharply limiting available coverage. Bennett gives the example of an AI-related loss capped at $500,000 under a policy whose overall face amount is $10 million, demonstrating that nominal policy limits may overstate protection for AI mistakes.
qs: Other policies—particularly property policies including real estate, land and inventory—also are starting to manage AI risks through the use of low sublimits, Bennett says.
For example, a loss from a single AI-related claim may be capped at $500,000 even though the policy has a face amount of $10 million.
There are two ways insurers limit their losses: by exclusions or by limiting the coverage amount, she says.

kp.k: Limited loss data obstructs broad AI insurance
kp.d: Kevin Kalinich says insurers must estimate the frequency and severity of AI losses before making coverage commercially viable. Unlike mature insurance markets, AI lacks the 20 to 30 years of actuarial modeling and loss-ratio data ordinarily used in underwriting, so widespread products remain limited.
qs: The insurance companies also need to establish the potential frequency and severity of AI losses, and they need to determine whether it’s possible to cover AI overall.
Typically, insurance companies will base their underwriting decisions on 20 to 30 years of actuarial modeling and loss ratio data.
They don’t have that amount of data on the frequency and severity of AI-related losses, Kalinich says.
While widespread AI insurance solutions are limited, there are some companies taking the first steps in this direction.

kp.k: Intangible AI risks are difficult to value
kp.d: Kalinich argues that intangible assets can offer insureds a higher potential return on insurance spending than tangible assets, but their lack of a clear market replacement value makes underwriting harder and can lead to negotiated or capped limits. His comparison assumes identical risk frequency and severity, which he explicitly identifies as a major assumption.
qs: The potential return on investment for insureds for policies addressing intangible assets often far exceeds that of tangible assets, he says.
That’s because tangible assets have a clear, market-determined replacement value, while intangible assets are harder to value, so coverage limits may be negotiated or capped.

kp.k: Insurance-backed AI products are beginning to emerge
kp.d: The article identifies early, specialized insurance models rather than comprehensive market-wide solutions. Orbital Witness offers clients optional protection for mistakes by its AI-driven residential-property product and reported no claims at the time of publication; it was considering expansion into commercial property transactions.
qs: Orbital Witness, a London-based company specializing in generative AI-driven due diligence for real estate transactions, collaborated with First Title Insurance to launch an insurance-backed guarantee for its residential property product.
If clients want to add the insurance, they pay a few dollars per policy and would be covered if the AI they use makes a mistake, Orbital Witness co-founder Ed Boulle says.
So far, they have had no claims, and they’re considering an expansion into commercial property transactions.

kp.k: Munich Re covers vendors and law-firm AI users
kp.d: Munich Re has offered its aiSure products since 2018, initially insuring AI vendors so they could compensate clients for underperformance. It subsequently broadened coverage to AI users, including law firms, offering protection for firms’ own financial losses and third-party liabilities such as lawsuits and associated costs.
qs: Meanwhile, Munich Re, a German multinational insurance company, has been writing insurance products to reduce uncertainties with regard to AI adoption since 2018 via its flagship aiSure product.

AiSure provides insurance to AI vendors, who can then offer insurance to their clients—with the promise to compensate the client if the AI tool didn’t perform, according to Michael Berger, the Palo Alto, California-based head of Munich Re’s Insure AI team.
Munich Re offers law firms using AI tools insurance coverage for their own financial losses stemming from AI, as well as coverage for third-party liabilities such as lawsuits and associated costs.

kp.k: AI underperformance now includes several emerging risks
kp.d: Michael Berger of Munich Re says the meaning of AI underperformance has expanded as AI adoption has changed. It now includes hallucination, intellectual-property infringement and systemic discrimination, prompting Munich Re to broaden its products from vendor-focused insurance toward coverage for AI users.
qs: In the last two years, the company has seen the nature and adoption of AI changing.
“The very definition of AI underperformance has changed to now include new risks like hallucination, [intellectual property] infringement or systemic discrimination,” he says.
“Our team considered it to be critical to respond to this changing risk profile by broadening our product offering to provide insurance coverage to AI users as well.”

kp.k: Coverage requires individualized AI-system due diligence
kp.d: Munich Re’s coverage is available to law firms, but not on standardized terms described in the article. The insurer reviews the AI systems used and then creates contract terms based on individual needs; pricing and further details were not disclosed.
qs: Their AI insurance is available across the board—including for law firms—but the individual process to gain coverage includes due diligence on the AI systems used.
Once that’s completed, contract details are created based on individual need.
Munich Re declined to provide more details and pricing.

kp.k: Insurers expect strong security and authentication controls
kp.d: The article recommends that insurers examine authentication, backup systems and safeguards for client documents before offering AI coverage. Bennett says insurers expect continuing personnel training, simulated phishing exercises and multilayer payment approvals with voice confirmation, tying insurability to firms’ operational cybersecurity practices.
qs: Before launching AI insurance for law firms, insurance companies should also determine the authentication protocols in place for access to the firm systems and have strong backup systems in place to maintain and secure access to client documents and other sensitive information.

“Insurers expect law firms to engage in constant vigilance in terms of training personnel with respect to the latest cybercrime tactics through security awareness training modules, simulated phishing exercises and multilayer approval processes to make payments with voice confirmation of payment instructions,” Bennett says.

kp.k: Vendor interdependence will receive deeper underwriting scrutiny
kp.d: Bennett predicts that outages and cyberattacks will lead insurers to investigate law firms’ vendor supply chains more closely. Underwriting may assess system interdependence and whether contractual indemnification and vendor insurance requirements adequately allocate risk.
qs: Also, as widespread cyber- and tech-related outages and attacks continue, insurers will remain focused on supply chain issues and may conduct deeper due diligence during the underwriting process into the law firm’s supply chain of vendors to assess interdependence of systems through contractual indemnification and insurance requirements with vendors, she adds.

kp.k: AI coverage must avoid overlapping insurance policies
kp.d: Melissa Ventrone argues that insurers need to design AI-specific plans only after becoming comfortable with firms’ supply-chain and authentication controls. Those plans must be coordinated with cyber-liability and intellectual-property insurance to prevent overlapping claims coverage.
qs: Finally, when the insurance companies are confident in the supply chain and authentication protocols, they will need to create an AI-related plan that doesn’t overlap with claims covered by cyber liability and intellectual property insurance policies, says Melissa Ventrone, the Chicago-based leader of the Cybersecurity, Data Protection and Privacy practice at Clark Hill.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Braff describes rapid generative-AI adoption and workload benefits, alongside unreliable outputs and an incomplete insurance response.
pts.d: Braff states that AI can accelerate mundane legal tasks and reduce workload but can produce hallucinations, biases and incomplete responses. Her central market claim is that comprehensive insurance arrangements for these risks are not yet widely available, despite emerging products.

pts.k: Lynda Bennett warns that existing malpractice and cyber policies may leave AI-related losses uncovered or subject to restrictive limits.
pts.d: Bennett says coverage depends on individual policy language: AI use may fall outside the definition of professional services, and sanctions associated with its use may not be covered. Cyber policies may provide relevant coverage, but their terms vary substantially. Her observation that property policies are beginning to use AI-related sublimits is a broader insurance-market claim, not a statement that all law-firm malpractice policies have such limits.

pts.k: Kevin Kalinich identifies missing loss history and difficult asset valuation as obstacles to developing commercially viable AI insurance.
pts.d: Kalinich says insurers need to establish the frequency and severity of AI losses and whether AI can be insured overall. Intangible assets are harder to value than tangible assets, so limits may be negotiated or capped. He illustrates a potentially higher return for insureds buying intangible-asset coverage, explicitly conditional on equal risk frequency and severity; this is an illustrative calculation, not observed AI-insurance performance.

pts.k: Ed Boulle and Michael Berger describe emerging products that transfer some AI-performance risks from users and vendors to insurers.
pts.d: Boulle reports that Orbital Witness and First Title Insurance offer an optional insurance-backed guarantee for AI-driven residential-property due diligence, with commercial-property expansion under consideration. Berger describes Munich Re's aiSure vendor coverage and its expansion to AI users as underperformance risks broaden to include hallucination, intellectual-property infringement and systemic discrimination. Braff reports that Munich Re offers law firms coverage for their own AI-related financial losses and third-party liabilities, subject to individualized underwriting.

pts.k: The article anticipates security- and vendor-focused underwriting, while Melissa Ventrone calls for coordination with existing cyber and intellectual-property coverage.
pts.d: Braff recommends examining authentication and backup arrangements before launching law-firm AI insurance. Bennett says insurers expect continuing staff security training and predicts sustained scrutiny of vendor supply chains, potentially including deeper due diligence into system interdependence, contractual indemnification and vendor insurance. Ventrone says AI coverage must be designed not to overlap with claims covered by cyber-liability and intellectual-property policies. These are underwriting expectations and recommendations, rather than measured effects of AI adoption.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source combines one adoption-budget statistic, a general expert-risk survey, insurance specialists' assessments and provider-reported product examples.
pts.d: Braff cites a February 2024 LexisNexis survey finding dedicated generative-AI budgets at 43% of Am Law 200 firms; this measures budgeting, not realized productivity or insurance losses. She also cites the World Economic Forum's 2024 survey of 1,500 experts and leaders as context for misinformation risk, not as legal-tool error-rate evidence. Coverage-gap and underwriting claims rely on Bennett's, Kalinich's and Ventrone's professional assessments. The concrete market examples come from Boulle and Berger; Orbital Witness's reported absence of claims is not accompanied by exposure or duration data, and Munich Re supplies no pricing detail. No productivity benchmark, adjudicated coverage dispute or quantified law-firm AI-loss study is presented.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The claims describe the market as of February 2025; future expansion and underwriting developments have no firm completion dates.
pts.d: The adoption statistic dates to February 2024. Munich Re's AI-insurance activity dates to 2018, with Berger describing changes over the preceding two years. Coverage availability is conditional on policy wording, exclusions, sublimits and, for Munich Re, AI-system due diligence and individualized contracts. Orbital Witness coverage is optional and currently described for residential property; commercial expansion is only being considered. Kalinich's reference to 20–30 years of customary loss data explains a current information gap, not a prediction that AI insurance must wait that long. His insurance-return illustration assumes equal risk frequency and severity.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The main affected groups are AI-using lawyers and firms, their clients, legal-AI vendors and insurers.
pts.d: Lawyers and firms may gain task efficiency while facing uninsured losses, sanctions-related coverage uncertainty, third-party claims and underwriting scrutiny of security practices and vendors. The Am Law 200 appears specifically in the budgeting evidence, not as the sole market exposed to these risks. Residential-property product clients can buy the reported Orbital Witness guarantee. AI vendors can use Munich Re coverage to offer performance compensation to clients, while law firms may obtain direct coverage for their own losses and liabilities. Insurers face uncertain loss distributions, valuation challenges and product-design questions. Orbital Witness is described as a legal-AI product company, not identified as an alternative legal service provider.
